title.en: Word order (SOV) and yes/no questions with क्या

summary.en: Hindi parks the verb at the end of the clause, keeps question words in place, and turns any statement into a yes/no question by placing क्या out front.

body.en:
From *आँगन हवेली*, season 1.

English builds sentences as Subject–Verb–Object ('I am Kavya', 'We use a register'). Hindi places the **verb at the end** (Subject–Object–Verb): *मैं काव्या हूँ* (`main kāvyā hūn`, literally 'I Kavya am') and *हम काग़ज़ का रजिस्टर इस्तेमाल करते हैं* ('We a paper register use'). Time and place expressions usually sit near the front (*आज सुबह* 'this morning', *दराज़ में* 'in the drawer'), while *नहीं* (`nahīn`, 'not') slips right before the verb.

Because the verb stays anchored at the end, **asking questions in Hindi requires zero word-order inversion**:

- **Yes/no questions:** Place *क्या* (`kyā`) right at the **beginning** of a statement and raise your pitch slightly at the end. Compare *दरवाज़ा बंद है* ('the door is closed') with Kavya's very first question: *क्या दरवाज़ा बंद है?* (`kyā darvāzā band hai?`, 'is the door closed?'). In fast, friendly conversation, speakers often drop *क्या* altogether and let rising intonation do the work: *और ये चाबियाँ हैं?* ('and these are the keys?').
- **'What?' vs yes/no *क्या*:** Position tells you which one you are hearing! At the very start of the sentence, *क्या* is an untranslated yes/no flag; **inside** the sentence right before the verb, *क्या* means **'what?'**: *तीसरी मंज़िल पर क्या है?* ('what is on the third floor?').
- **Other question words**—*कहाँ* ('where?'), *कौन* ('who?'), *क्यों* ('why?'), *कैसे* / *कैसा* ('how / what kind?'), *कितने* ('how many?')—likewise sit right in the slot of the answer: *कंप्यूटर कहाँ है?* ('the computer where is?').
